400.title: Pauri 40, sound: anad sunahu
400.hook: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore
400.howItsDone: At the close of most Sikh services and ceremonies, the sangat sings six pauris of the Anand, the first five and the fortieth, before Ardas; many Sikhs also recite all forty pauris as part of their morning prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gur prasaad, and your line, grace gives. Did you take one gift without evening the account? Today is day four hundred on this path. Thank you for walking it. And today, the last pauri of the Anand. Day four hundred.

Some songs end by turning to face the room. The singer stops singing about something and starts singing to the people in front of her. Anand Sahib does that in its last pauri. After thirty-nine stanzas, the fortieth opens with a call: two short words and then a long one, the way you'd call across a crowded hall to get everyone's attention. You've already learned the sound of the Anand's first pauri. Today, the sound of the fortieth, the one that closes the whole song of bliss. Today: vaddabhaageeho.
screen: `A SONG TURNS TO FACE THE ROOM.` → `THE LAST PAURI OPENS WITH A CALL.` → `TODAY: THE SOUND OF THE FORTIETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, slowly: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore. Take it in pieces. Anad: a-NUD. Notice it's not quite anand, the word in the title of the whole song. The Gurmukhi here is written without the nasal sound, anad, a short, open word. Then sunahu: su-NA-hu, three soft syllables, and it's a call: hear. Then the long one: vaddabhaageeho. Vadd, with the tongue curled back a little for the d, then bhaa, then gee, then ho: vadd-BHAA-gee-ho. It's a word for a group of people, said as if calling across a room. Then sagal: sa-GAL, all. Manorath: ma-NO-rath. And poore: POO-re, two beats, the last one light. Put it together: anad sunahu, vaddabhaageeho, sagal manorath poore. Hear how it moves. Two short words like a knock on the door, a long word that opens it, and then a line that lands. Many ragis sing it to a tune that lifts on vaddabhaageeho and settles on poore. The pauri goes on for five more lines and ends, the way Guru Amar Das ends so many, with the name Nanak and a sound of its own: the unstruck music playing. That's tomorrow. For today, let the first line get into your mouth. And this is the pauri the sangat sings after the first five at the close of services, so it's a line many Sikhs have sung hundreds of times. Anad sunahu.
screen: `ANAD: A-NUD, NOT QUITE ANAND.` · `SUNAHU: SU-NA-HU, A CALL.` · `VADDABHAAGEEHO: VADD-BHAA-GEE-HO.` · `SAGAL MANORATH POORE: A LINE THAT LANDS.` · then, large: `ANAD SUNAHU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the first line aloud. Not perfectly, just aloud. Anad sunahu. Pause. Vaddabhaageeho. Pause. Sagal manorath poore. Say it again, a little slower, and listen to your own voice the way you'd listen to someone else's. If you know the tune, you can hum it. Then let the line go and rest in the quiet it leaves behind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once at the end. The bell holds the time.
Vaddabhaageeho, you of great fortune. The last pauri of the Anand, sung with the first five at the close of Sikh services and ceremonies. It begins: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore.
Your line: anad sunahu. Today, say it once under your breath at some point you'd normally rush past, a doorway, a red light. Day four hundred.

screen: `DAY 400 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PAURI 40, MEANING: HEAR THE BLISS.`

401.title: Pauri 40, meaning: hear the bliss
401.hook: hear the song of bliss, fortunate ones; all longings are fulfilled (Anand 40)
401.howItsDone: The fortieth pauri is sung with the first five at the close of Sikh services and ceremonies, and is the last pauri of the full Anand Sahib that many Sikhs recite each morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri forty, and your line, anad sunahu. Can you still say the first line? Anad sunahu, vaddabhaageeho, sagal manorath poore. Today, what it means. Day four hundred one.

A sticky note on the fridge, a list of things wanted. A job. A test result. A phone call from someone. A child who sleeps through the night. Cross one off and two more get added underneath. Then someone calls out across a crowded hall: listen, you lucky ones, every one of those longings is met. That's how the last pauri of the Anand begins. Today: manorath.
screen: `A LIST OF THINGS WANTED.` → `CROSS ONE OFF, TWO MORE APPEAR.` → `LISTEN, LUCKY ONES: ALL LONGINGS MET.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, in paraphrase. Anad sunahu: hear the bliss. Vaddabhaageeho: you of great fortune. Sagal manorath poore: all longings are fulfilled. Then the pauri says how. The Supreme Lord has been found, and every anxiety is gone. Pain, sickness and suffering leave, it says, by hearing the true bani. The saints and friends are delighted, because they've come to know it through the perfect Guru. Then a line that echoes a pauri we heard nine days ago. Back in pauri twenty-four, unripe were the speakers and unripe the hearers. Here, at the end, it flips: pure are those who hear, holy are those who speak, and the True Guru fills everything. The Anand closes with Nanak's prayer, at the Guru's feet, and a sound: the unstruck music, anahad, playing on and on, like trumpets nobody is blowing. So what does every longing met mean? Not that the list gets checked off. The pauri is sung by people who still have bills, illnesses and phone calls that don't come. The pauri says the longings are fulfilled because the One they were all reaching for has been found. The list was a long way of wanting one thing. Some Sikhs hear in this why the Anand is sung at the close of every gathering: whatever the occasion was about, the song ends where all the longings end. Every longing met.
screen: `HEAR THE BLISS, YOU FORTUNATE ONES.` · `THE LORD FOUND, EVERY ANXIETY GONE.` · `PURE ARE THE HEARERS, HOLY THE SPEAKERS.` · `THE UNSTRUCK MUSIC PLAYS ON.` · then, large: `EVERY LONGING MET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to the last pauri whole. If you can find a recording of the six pauris, play the final one, from anad sunahu to the end, and just let it pass through you. If you can't, sit with the first line: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore. Bring one longing from your list to mind, and set it gently beside the line. Not to cancel it. Just to see it in that light. Then breathe. The bell holds the time.
Manorath, a longing. The last pauri of the Anand: hear the bliss, fortunate ones, all manorath are fulfilled; pure are the hearers, holy the speakers; the unstruck music plays.
Your line: every longing met. Today, when you catch yourself adding to the list, pause, and ask what you're really reaching for underneath it. Day four hundred one.

trapdoor: what you thought: every longing met means God gives you everything you want.
what it means: the longings are fulfilled because the One they were all reaching for has been found.

what a scholar hears: the final pauri mirrors pauri 24's pairing, unripe speakers and hearers becoming pure ones, and closes on anahad, the unstruck sound, a term with a long history in Indian devotional and yogic language.

402.title: At every ceremony
402.hook: births, weddings, deaths and every service end with the six pauris and Ardas
402.howItsDone: Sikh services and ceremonies, including the Anand Karaj wedding, the naming of a child and the bhog after a death, close with six pauris of the Anand, Ardas said standing, and the sharing of karah prashad.

segments.voice: Yesterday, manorath, and your line, every longing met. Did you ask what you were really reaching for? Today, where those six pauris actually get sung. Day four hundred two.

Notice how things end. A phone call trails off: okay, so, yeah, anyway, bye. A meeting ends when someone has to be somewhere else. A party ends when the last guest finds their coat. Plenty of endings just happen. In a Sikh community, the big days of a life end in a way that's been decided in advance, and it's the same way every time, whether the day was a wedding or a funeral. Today: Anand Karaj.
screen: `OKAY, SO, YEAH, ANYWAY, BYE.` → `PLENTY OF ENDINGS JUST HAPPEN.` → `THESE ENDINGS ARE CHOSEN, EVERY TIME.`

segments.voice: Go to a Sikh wedding. The couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib four times while the four laavan are sung. Then the sangat sings six pauris of the Anand, the first five and the fortieth, and everyone stands for Ardas. The ceremony itself is called Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss, and in 1909 the British government in India passed an Anand Marriage Act recognizing it. Go to a naming. The Guru Granth Sahib is opened, a name is chosen from the first letter of the hymn it opens to, and again, the six pauris and Ardas. Go to an ordinary Sunday program, with an hour of kirtan and a talk. It ends the same way. And go, if you ever have to, to the bhog that closes the reading of the Guru Granth Sahib after someone has died. The six pauris are there too. Tradition says Guru Amar Das composed the Anand around the birth of a grandson, who was named Anand. So it began at a birth, and now it's sung at deaths too. That's the striking part. Singing a song of bliss at a funeral isn't pretending nothing hurts. Sikh teaching speaks of hukam, the order of the One, and Sikhs who sing the six pauris at a death speak of it as accepting that order with trust, even through tears. Whatever the day held, joy or grief, it's handed back the same way: bliss sung together, and then Ardas, standing. A life marked by many ceremonies ends each one in the same place. End in bliss.
screen: `A WEDDING: LAAVAN, THEN THE SIX PAURIS.` · `A NAMING, A SUNDAY: THE SAME ENDING.` · `EVEN AFTER A DEATH, THE ANAND.` · `JOY OR GRIEF, HANDED BACK THE SAME WAY.` · then, large: `END IN BLISS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how you end things. Think back over yesterday. How did your conversations end? Your meals? Your work? Your day, the last thing before sleep? Don't judge any of it. Just notice whether endings happened to you, or whether you chose them. Then pick one ending coming up today, a call, a meal, the workday, and decide now how you'd like it to close. A thank you. A breath. A moment of quiet. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss. Sikh weddings, namings, Sunday services and the bhog after a death all end the same way: six pauris of the Anand, then Ardas.
Your line: end in bliss. Today, close one ordinary thing on purpose, a call, a meal, a shift, with a real thank you instead of an anyway. Day four hundred two.

403.title: Anand at dusk
403.hook: the six pauris also sit inside the evening Rehras
403.howItsDone: Many Sikhs add the full Anand Sahib to their morning banis, and the evening Rehras Sahib includes its six pauris, the first five and the fortieth, before Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand Karaj, and your line, end in bliss. Did you close one ordinary thing on purpose? Today, the same six pauris, not at a ceremony, but at the end of an ordinary day. Day four hundred three.

Play a song you love at seven in the morning, on the way to work, coffee in hand. Then play the same song at seven in the evening, shoes off, lights low. It's the same recording, note for note. But it isn't the same song. In the morning it pushes you out the door. In the evening it brings you home. A Sikh who keeps the daily prayers meets the Anand twice a day, in two different lights. Today: anand bhaiaa.
screen: `ONE SONG AT 7 A.M.` → `THE SAME SONG AT 7 P.M.` → `THE ANAND, TWICE A DAY.`

segments.voice: In the morning, the Rehat Maryada names the Japji, Jaap Sahib and the savaiyas, and many Sikhs add the whole Anand, all forty pauris, to those morning banis. That's the full meal. Then evening comes, and with it Rehras, the evening prayer, which we'll walk through line by line starting in two days. Near its end, Rehras carries the same six pauris you now know: the first five, and the fortieth. So the Anand frames the day. It's there at the start, in full, and it returns at dusk, shorter, like a taste of the morning's meal. Think about what the first line sounds like at each end. Anand bhaiaa meree maae: joy has come, my mother, I have found the True Guru. In the morning, that line goes out into the day ahead, before anything has gone right or wrong. At dusk, the day has happened. The bus was late. Someone was unkind. Something good came out of nowhere. And still the same words come: joy has come, mother. Not because the day was perfect. The line says where the joy comes from: I have found the True Guru. Not from the day. That's why it can be sung at both ends. Some families sing the evening pauris together, standing in a kitchen, or sitting on the floor of a front room with the lamps just lit. Some say them alone on a train home. The words don't change. The light does. Dusk, with joy.
screen: `MORNING: ALL FORTY PAURIS.` · `DUSK: THE SIX PAURIS INSIDE REHRAS.` · `THE SAME FIRST LINE AT BOTH ENDS.` · `THE JOY: FROM THE GURU, NOT THE DAY.` · then, large: `DUSK, WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hum the first pauri at dusk. If it's evening where you are, look at the light outside. If it isn't, just picture the sky going orange. Then hum, or softly say, the first line: anand bhaiaa meree maae, satguroo mai paaiaa. Joy has come, my mother, I have found the True Guru. Let your whole day so far stand behind the words, the good and the bad. Say it, or hum it, two or three times. Then rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Anand bhaiaa, joy has come. The six pauris of the Anand return inside Rehras, the evening prayer, so the song of bliss frames the Sikh day at both ends.
Your line: dusk, with joy. Tonight, as the light goes, hum anand bhaiaa once, whatever kind of day it was. Day four hundred three.

404.title: Anand close
404.hook: forty pauris of joy that is steady, not giddy
404.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the full Anand Sahib each morning and its six pauris in the evening Rehras and at the close of every service and ceremony, and they often describe its joy as sahaj: steady, poised and not dependent on circumstance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anand bhaiaa, and your line, dusk, with joy. Did you hum anand bhaiaa as the light went? Today we close the Anand, after twenty-five days inside it. Day four hundred four.

Diwali night in a Punjabi neighborhood. Fireworks go up, crack open, flood the sky with color, and in two seconds they're gone, leaving smoke and a ringing in the ears. Below them, on a windowsill, a small clay lamp burns. Nobody films the lamp. But it's still burning at midnight, long after the last rocket. Both are a kind of joy. Only one of them lasts the night. For forty pauris, the Anand has been singing about the second kind. Today: sahaj.
screen: `FIREWORKS: TWO SECONDS OF COLOR.` → `A CLAY LAMP ON THE SILL.` → `STILL BURNING AT MIDNIGHT.`

segments.voice: Look back at where we've walked. The Anand opened with joy found, and a word for how it was found: sahaj, easily, with poise. That word sets the tone for everything. Then: man meriaa; what is there that isn't in Your house; the true Name my support. Giaan anjan: everyone talks of bliss, but it's known through the Guru. It's given, not grabbed, and chaturaaee never found it. Sahsaa: the Word clears doubt. Khanniahu tikhee: the devotees' way is sharper than a sword. The treasure is within. Without the True Guru, words are unripe. Then the body, the eyes and the ears, each told the Lord's light is in them, and the breath played like music in the cave of the body. Gur prasaad: grace gives the Word. And the last pauri: hear the bliss, every longing met, the unstruck music playing on. Then we followed the six pauris out into life: weddings, namings, Sundays, the bhog after a death, and dusk at the end of an ordinary day. So what kind of joy is this? Not giddy. It doesn't depend on the day going well, which is why it can be sung at a funeral. It isn't excitement, which burns out. Sahaj is a steadiness, a balance, the lamp rather than the firework. Guru Amar Das wrote a song of bliss that a person could sing in a hospital corridor and mean it. That's the joy the Anand is about: steady, because it rests on the One, not on what happens next. Steady joy.
screen: `SAHAJ: JOY FOUND WITH EASE AND POISE.` · `GIVEN, NOT GRABBED; THE TREASURE WITHIN.` · `BODY, EYES, EARS, BREATH: LIGHT IN ALL.` · `SUNG AT EVERY CEREMONY, AT BOTH ENDS.` · then, large: `STEADY JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your steadiest joy. Not the biggest, not the most exciting. The steadiest. Something that's been quietly good in your life through good weeks and bad ones. A friendship. A morning cup of tea. A faith. The sound of a particular voice. Find it, and name it to yourself in a few words. Then sit with it the way you'd sit beside a small lamp, not doing anything, just near the light. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.

Sahaj, steadiness and poise. Forty pauris by Guru Amar Das: joy found through the Guru, given by grace, light in body, eyes and ears, sung at every ceremony and at both ends of the day. A joy that's steady, not giddy.
Your line: steady joy. Today, check in once with your steadiest joy, the lamp, not the firework. Tomorrow we begin Rehras, the evening prayer. Day four hundred four.

405.title: Provisions for the road
405.hook: Rehras is said as work ends, like provisions for the night's journey
405.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib in the evening as the day's work ends, at home or in the gurdwara, often followed by Ardas; the Rehat Maryada lists its contents as nine shabads, the Benti Chaupai, a savaiya and dohra, six pauris of the Anand, the Mundavani and a slok.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sahaj, and your line, steady joy. Did you check in with your steadiest joy? Today a new stretch of the path begins: the evening prayer. Day four hundred five.

Late afternoon at a truck stop on the Grand Trunk Road. A driver is getting ready for the night run to Delhi. He fills a steel tiffin with rotis and dal, tops up a bottle of water, checks the tires, wipes the windshield. Nobody would set out on a long dark road without packing first. The night is coming whether he's ready or not, so he gets ready. Sikhs have a prayer for exactly this moment of the day. Today: check the tiffin.
screen: `A TRUCK STOP, LATE AFTERNOON.` → `A TIFFIN PACKED FOR THE NIGHT RUN.` → `NOBODY SETS OUT WITHOUT PACKING.`

segments.voice: The evening prayer is called Rehras. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, says it's recited in the evening, when the day's work is done. The name is often explained from two old words: rah, the road or the way, and raas, the goods or capital a traveler carries. Provisions for the road. Some teachers also hear in it a humble petition, the request of someone setting out. Scholars discuss the exact roots, but the picture Sikhs give is clear: the day is a journey, night is the next stretch of it, and Rehras is what you pack. What's in the tiffin? In the standard Rehat Maryada order, it begins with nine shabads from the opening pages of the Guru Granth Sahib. Five are grouped under the heading So Dar, the door, and four under So Purakh, that Being. Then come the Benti Chaupai of Guru Gobind Singh, a short savaiya and a dohra, the six pauris of the Anand you've just learned, and two closing passages that end the Guru Granth Sahib itself, the Mundavani and a slok. Some Sikh traditions recite a longer form, with more hymns added. Then, in many homes, Ardas. Over the next two weeks we'll unpack it, one piece a day, the same way we walked through the Anand. For now, just notice the shape of the Sikh day. Morning prayers before the work starts. Rehras as the work ends. Provisions for the road.
screen: `REHRAS: SAID AS THE DAY'S WORK ENDS.` · `RAH AND RAAS: THE ROAD AND ITS GOODS.` · `SO DAR, SO PURAKH, CHAUPAI, ANAND.` · `PACKED FOR THE NIGHT'S STRETCH.` · then, large: `PROVISIONS FOR THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause at dusk. Right now, wherever the sun is, imagine the end of your workday: the laptop closing, the apron coming off, the last email sent. Let your shoulders drop as if it's already happened. Take a slow breath and ask: what do I need for the next stretch, the evening, the night? Rest? Patience? Someone's voice? Let the answer come without forcing it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, and let that be the first thing packed. The bell holds the time.
Rehras. The Sikh evening prayer, said as the day's work ends, often explained as provisions for the road: shabads, the Chaupai and the Anand, packed for the night.
Your line: check the tiffin. Today, as your work ends, take one minute to pause before the evening starts, like a driver checking the tiffin. Day four hundred five.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rehras is just the name of a Sikh evening hymn.
what it means: a whole evening prayer said as work ends, packed like provisions for the night's stretch of the road.

what a scholar hears: the name is commonly derived from Persian rah, road, and raas, capital or goods, and its standard contents are set out in the Sikh Rehat Maryada, though some traditions recite a longer form.

406.title: So dar: the door, again
406.hook: so dar: what is that door where You sit and care for all, sung at dusk (Asa, ang 8–9)
406.howItsDone: So Dar is the first shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited in the evening; a near-identical version is pauri 27 of the Japji in the morning, so many Sikhs sing this hymn at both ends of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rehras, and your line, check the tiffin. Did you pause for a minute as your work ended? Today, the first thing in the tiffin, and it's something you've met before. Day four hundred six.

You come home in the evening and stop at your own front door, keys in hand. You've walked through it a thousand times. But tonight, for some reason, you notice it: the scuff at the bottom, the light from inside showing round the edges, the sound of someone cooking. The same door you left by this morning looks different coming home. Rehras opens with a door, and it's one the Japji already showed us at the start of the day. Today: so dar, the door, again.
screen: `KEYS IN HAND AT YOUR OWN DOOR.` → `THE SAME DOOR, A DIFFERENT LIGHT.` → `REHRAS OPENS WITH A DOOR.`

segments.voice: The first shabad of Rehras, by Guru Nanak in Raag Asa, opens with a question. So dar keha, so ghar keha: what is that door, what is that house, where You sit and take care of all? Almost the same hymn is pauri twenty-seven of the Japji, the morning prayer. The Guru Granth Sahib carries it more than once, and Sikhs who keep the daily banis sing it at both ends of the day. At dawn, inside the Japji. At dusk, as the first thing in Rehras. Then the shabad answers its own question, not with an address but with a crowd. Countless instruments play at that door, it says in paraphrase, and countless musicians. Wind, water and fire sing. The gods of the old stories sing, and the record keepers of the dead, and the scholars, the warriors, the saints. Whole worlds and galaxies sing. Those who please You sing, Guru Nanak says, steeped in love, and there are more than anyone could think of. And it closes on who sits at that door: the True One, who is and always will be, who made everything, who needs no one's orders, the King above kings. Nanak remains within His will. So Rehras doesn't begin by asking for anything. It begins by standing at the door at dusk and hearing that everything is already singing there. The door, again, at the other end of the day.
screen: `SO DAR KEHA: WHAT IS THAT DOOR?` · `THE SAME HYMN AS JAPJI 27.` · `WIND, FIRE, SAINTS, WORLDS: ALL SINGING.` · `THE KING OF KINGS; NANAK IN HIS WILL.` · then, large: `THE DOOR AT DUSK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a doorway at dusk. If you can, go and stand near a door: the front door, a bedroom door, even an open window. If not, picture the door you'll come through tonight. Look at it as if for the first time. Notice the light on each side of it: the dusk out there, the lamps in here. Stand, in your mind, on the line between them, where the shabad stands to ask its question. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
So dar. That door: Guru Nanak's question that opens Rehras, sung also in the Japji. This week: pauri forty, every ceremony, the Anand at dusk and its close, Rehras, and now the door.
Your line: the door at dusk. Tonight, when you walk through your own door, pause on the threshold for one breath and listen. Day four hundred six.

original.note: Gurmukhi: so dar, that door; the opening words of Rehras and of Japji pauri 27.

trapdoor: what you thought: so dar is about the door of a gurdwara.
what it means: Guru Nanak's question about the door where the One sits and cares for all, answered by everything singing there.
what a scholar hears: the So Dar hymn is recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib in more than one place, as Japji 27 and in Raag Asa, with small differences of wording.
